cells.tense: You are holding a structure steady while it is still taking shape around you.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to whoever is building alongside you, which part of this is still open and which part is settled.
cells.core:
The thing you're building is at the stage where it needs holding more than it needs pushing. You've got the weight of it — the unfinished parts, the parts that don't fit yet — and you're carrying that without going stiff about it. That's not the same as waiting. It's what lets the thing keep its shape while it's still soft.

It works because you can take the pressure without passing it on, and because you've stopped needing to know how it ends before you keep going. That last part is what keeps this from turning into force. Stay close to the people building it with you — this came out of something you cleared together. Keep letting the parts that are still open be open, and keep asking whether the shape you're holding is the one that serves the people under it. Carrying it steady is the work right now.
cells.sheetLine: You hold the shape while it's still soft, and that's the work.
cells.verb: building something new from what the clearing revealed, with more than one pair of hands
cells.place: where you hold form under pressure without hardening

cells.tense: You are bracing against a future that cannot be written in yet, and the bracing is showing.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're already carrying and put it down for a day — tell whoever needs to know it's theirs until tomorrow.
cells.core:
You're holding a future that hasn't arrived, and you're holding it hard. The structure isn't finished, so you're gripping every edge of it before it's built — checking it will stand, checking it will hold, checking it won't come apart in your hands. Some of that pressure is being spent on loads that aren't yours yet.

Endurance is supposed to be the thing that keeps you steady under a real load. Right now it's working on loads that haven't shown up, and the effort of that is showing in how you hold everything. Set one thing down. Not long — just long enough to find out it doesn't need you holding it. What you're carrying was going to be carried by more than you anyway. You can put the shape back together after you've stood next to it instead of under it.

cells.tense: You stopped reaching for the work a while back, and you're still standing where you stopped.
cells.ask: Name the one thing worth building and tell one person it's yours to build — then take one step where someone can see you do it.
cells.core:
There's a structure you know how to raise and you've stopped raising it. You were holding it once — the weight, the unfinished parts, the thing taking shape — and now you've stepped back. What you had for bearing that kind of weight is still there. It just isn't being spent on anything.

Don't try to feel your way back into it. Feeling came after the doing last time, not before. Go to what's yours and say it plainly, in front of someone, in a way that doesn't leave you room to take it back. What you say out loud is what holds your direction when resistance shows up — and resistance will show up. You don't have to feel like it again before you move on it. Moving first is what brings the rest back, one step at a time, where it can be seen.
cells.sheetLine: You know how to build it. You stopped. Start with one step.

cells.tense: The building is already happening through your hands, and you keep calling it something else.
cells.ask: Take one piece of this you've been calling the group's or the moment's and say to yourself, once, plainly, that you made it.
cells.core:
You're raising something — holding the weight while it takes shape, keeping the unfinished parts from collapsing — and you talk about it like it's happening to you. The structure is going up. The person holding it steady isn't claiming the place.

There's no gap in the work. There's a gap between the work and the account you give of it, and that account is costing you the standing the building would give you. It's not modesty. It's a direction you haven't owned out loud, and directions that don't get owned don't survive a hard month. Say it once, without softening it — that this is yours, that you chose the shape. Then check whether the shape still feels like yours now that you've said so. If it doesn't, that's the real finding, and it's worth having.
cells.sheetLine: You're already building it. You keep calling it someone else's.
cells.verb: building something new from what the clearing revealed, with more than one pair of hands
cells.place: where you hold form under pressure without hardening

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is actively building something new right now — the record gives a capacity for skilled construction under pressure, not a project on the bench; a reader could fairly say nothing is currently being raised. The ask survives being wrong because it acts on whatever is already being held, not on a specific build, and stays useful as a way of testing whether the structure serves the people inside it. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you're meant to lead' — authority is the medicine's frame, not the person's fact, and it stays out. Write as the record, not as a verdict on their life.
